title: Is This the End of Cheap Salmon?
text:
A few decades ago, Americans thought eating salmon meant picking bones from tins of Alaskan fillets or indulging in luxury dishes such as pounded escalopes in sorrel sauce. These days, Cava offers pomegranate-glazed salmon in its bowls; Sweetgreen’s is lacquered in miso. At supermarkets, shoppers can buy individually portioned, ready-to-eat fillets; airports and gas stations stock premade salmon bowls.

 Salmon’s ascent didn’t happen by accident. When Norwegian fish breeders, farmers, and businesspeople learned to raise a wild fish in massive underwater pens, exporters worked hard to sell Americans on farmed Atlantic salmon. (They also convinced Japanese consumers to overcome their aversion to raw salmon in sushi.) In 2025, the U.S. imported more than half a million metric tons of salmon—not just from Norway, but from Chile, Scotland, and other producers—and food marketers want to create yet more occasions for eating salmon, at your desk, between flights, or after a workout. Frequent seafood consumers have come to expect the fish whenever they want it.

 The people producing that salmon aren’t so sure they can continue to deliver. The fish have a complicated life cycle, and for decades, the world’s largest aquaculture firms have been producing ever more fillets from the particular ecology in which salmon can be farmed. “But you never know what nature brings,” Krister Hoaas, the head of communication and policy at the industry group Seafood Norway, told me. Disease, parasites, and warming waters all constrain salmon supply. In its quarterly earnings report, released this past August, the salmon producer Mowi cited a forecast of no growth in the global supply of farmed Atlantic salmon during the second half of 2026, followed by little or no growth in 2027. The industry is also facing new demand from China, where the volume of salmon imports grew by 50 percent last year. The world simply might not be able to produce as much salmon as people want to eat.

 Salmon producers certainly want to farm more fish, but that means getting millions of them through a perilous year or more at sea. This July, I walked vertiginously along the circumference of a salmon pen off the west coast of Norway. The pen, roughly the size of a baseball infield, was linked by plastic feed pipes and power lines to five others like it; hundreds of thousands of salmon swam in loose circles below the surface.

 A modern salmon pen is as much an industrial marvel as a data center. A cluster of five or six pens can hold more than 1 million fish. The salmon arrive after smolting, a physiological transformation that prepares their bodies for life in salt water. The pens are anchored in cold, deep waters like the ones in which wild salmon spend some of their adult lives. Watched by underwater cameras, they are fed pellets made of grains, soy, red pigment, and smaller fish. Over the course of one to two years, they grow large enough to transport to shore for processing.

 The fish that make their way to butchering—and from there into vacuum packs, bowls, and salads the world over—have overcome uncertain odds. Like broiler chickens, they’ve been selectively bred to produce abundant, delicious flesh. Some salmon develop a viral disease that ruptures their hearts; others, known as “losers,” linger near the surface, barely responding to food. There are other fundamental challenges in bringing farmed salmon to harvest. The fish are vulnerable to sea lice, tiny parasites that feed on their skin; treatments to remove them can injure or kill the fish. Tens of millions of farmed salmon die in Norway’s ocean pens each year before reaching slaughter weight, a loss that troubles both animal-welfare advocates and producers.

 Livestock farming has a wide geographic range: Pigs, chickens, and cows can be raised nearly anywhere. But farmed salmon require specific ecological niches: cool, well-circulating water with plenty of oxygen, enough depth for large nets, and shelter from waves. Today, Norway and Chile produce about four-fifths of the world’s farmed Atlantic salmon, and both restrict how much can be raised and where. Warming waters add another complication. In southern Norway, higher temperatures have helped sea lice multiply faster, forcing farmers to treat their fish more often.

 The salmon industry has transformed itself before, breeding faster-growing fish, nearly eliminating antibiotic use in Norwegian production, and replacing much of the fish in its feed with plants. (In 2025, European producers started including poultry by-products in their feed, a practice whose adoption had been slowed by European supermarket restrictions and presumed consumer queasiness about fish eating chicken.) Big producers are working on getting more fish and flesh from existing farms by keeping young fish in tanks on land for longer or, once they’re in the ocean, and submerging the pens deeper beneath the surface to protect against lice.

 How much more salmon the world can produce remains uncertain. The industry is confident of growing demand, though, particularly in populous Asian countries where even a small shift in eating habits could bring millions of new customers. Salmon imports in the Asia-Pacific rose nearly 12 percent last year, with China, Thailand, and South Korea leading growth in purchases of fresh whole fish. In the very near future, more people could be competing to eat the same amount of fish.

 The world has faced a version of this problem before, when salmon production dipped. Grocers and restaurants have to reconcile what foods cost with what shoppers will pay, and that gap makes salmon an unusually fickle fish, according to Boston Consulting Group’s 2025 report on salmon demand. In 2022, as global production contracted, supermarkets’ purchasing costs rose faster than their selling prices. Salmon imports from Chile, generally cheaper than those from Norway, sheltered American retailers, but some European grocers cut their selection, stopped paying for enticing price cuts, or removed salmon from stores in poorer neighborhoods.

 Last year, an unexpected bumper harvest in global Atlantic salmon production brought some relief. But if production struggles to keep pace with appetites in the U.S. and abroad, American shoppers could see fewer salmon specials at the seafood counter and a narrower selection in the refrigerated case. Chains such as Cava and Sweetgreen would have to make their own calculation: How much more will customers pay to select salmon as their protein? (And at what price would most of them choose chicken instead?) For diners and shoppers able to absorb higher prices, salmon could remain a regular part of a weekday lunch. For those whose budgets are already stretched, salmon might require a special occasion again.

 The limits on salmon production have inspired a raft of experiments. In July, I sailed with Erlend Eide, the co-owner of Eide Fjordbruk, to WaterMoon, a facility in Norway where salmon were being raised in an underwater enclosure designed to keep out sea lice. (A rupture in the membrane last month led to the location’s closure.) Over Zoom, Andreas Thorud, the managing director of a Norwegian Chinese salmon firm in Ningbo, China, showed me the beautiful, silvery fish being harvested from land-based tanks nearby. Justin Kolbeck, a co-founder and the CEO of Wildtype, proposes dispensing with the rest of the fish altogether and growing salmon cells on nutrients he describes as “slightly expensive Gatorade.” The limit, he told me, is financing: “If there was capital available, we’d be in your Whole Foods.” The rewards for solving the problem of salmon supply are immense. The industry has become very good at convincing people to want what it raises, and as more people around the world can afford more protein, they, too, want some of it to be salmon.
